problem: Different clients can hold different label errors, and correcting them must fit the devices’ available computation.
contribution: FedLN estimates client noise and offers three alternative interventions: label correction, adaptive distillation, or noise-aware aggregation.
reading_guide: Compare noise patterns within each dataset: the strongest correction method under random noise can fail under class flipping.

diagram.title: Three choices for noisy labels
diagram.description: Choose one FedLN intervention. NNC corrects local labels before training; AKD adds teacher supervision during local training; NA-FedAvg reweights client updates on the server.

stages.title: NNC
stages.detail: Use pretrained embeddings and neighborhood voting to correct labels before federated training.

stages.title: AKD
stages.detail: Add teacher supervision when estimated client noise exceeds a threshold.

stages.title: NA-FedAvg
stages.detail: Estimate noise from one round of energy scores, then reduce noisier clients’ aggregation weights.

diagram.footnote: These are alternatives, not sequential steps. NNC and embedding-based AKD use pretrained representations; NA-FedAvg sends energy scores to the server once.

results.title: When label correction helps—and fails
results.question: How do the three alternatives respond to different noise structures?
results.context: CIFAR-10, ResNet-20; 70% label noise on 80% of 30 clients; 200 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation. Test accuracy (%), higher is better; mean of three runs, no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: NNC leads under random noise but falls below FedAvg under class flipping; AKD and NA-FedAvg remain above FedAvg in both selected columns.
results.caveat: Columns fix noise level at 70% and change sparsity from 0% to 100%. FedCorr uses its additional preprocessing and fine-tuning schedule; these are accuracy comparisons, not equal-cost comparisons.

results.title: The same boundary in audio
results.question: Does the contrast also appear in keyword recognition?
results.context: Speech Commands v2, 12 classes, convolutional audio model; 70% label noise on 80% of 30 clients; 200 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation. Test accuracy (%), higher is better; mean of three runs, no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: NNC performs strongly with dispersed noise, while NA-FedAvg has the highest accuracy among these methods under class flipping.
results.caveat: The embedding methods use TRILLsson representations. FedCorr was not evaluated for audio because the authors did not use its MixUp-based procedure for that task.

results.title: When every client is noisy
results.question: How dependent is noise-aware aggregation on clients with clean labels?
results.context: CIFAR-10, ResNet-20; 40% random label noise per noisy client, sparsity 0%; 30 clients, 200 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation. Test accuracy (%), higher is better; mean of three runs, no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: NNC changes little in this sweep; NA-FedAvg loses accuracy as the population of clients with clean labels disappears.
results.caveat: 100% noisy clients means every client has 40% corrupted labels. It does not mean every label is wrong.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, PathMNIST, EuroSAT, Speech Commands v2, and human-annotated CIFAR-10N/100N.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: ResNet-20 and an audio CNN; ConvMixer-128/4 checks on CIFAR-10 and EuroSAT. CLIP ViT-B/32 or TRILLsson provides embeddings.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: FedAvg, label smoothing, bi-tempered loss, Confident Learning, and FedCorr on vision tasks.

evaluation.label: Protocol
evaluation.value: Flower simulation; random client partitions with quantity imbalance; three runs per setting. Human-noise experiments use the original clean test sets.

limitations: NNC can reinforce incorrect neighborhood majorities under severe class flipping; useful embeddings alone do not ensure correct label votes.
NA-FedAvg degrades when clean clients disappear and requires all clients to supply scores for its noise-estimation round.
Most tests inject class-conditional synthetic label noise; the real human-noise evaluation is confined to CIFAR-10N/100N.
Client-resource arguments are supported by algorithm design; measurements of computation and energy on real devices are left for future work.
takeaways: The noise pattern matters as much as the noise rate when choosing a correction strategy.
Teacher embeddings can supervise a model without forcing a potentially incorrect replacement label.
Noise-aware aggregation reduces client-side requirements but depends on distinguishing relatively reliable clients.
